title: Field-mapper JSON mode + tool-routing demo with HavenBio
customer_attendees: Dr. Elena Ruiz (Head of Data Science)
summary: Redwood AE+SE walked HavenBio through JSON mode, field-mapper schemas, and tool-routing. Demo focused on deterministic output contracts, routing to a custom internal tool for record enrichment, and fallback policies to cheaper quantized variants. Customer raised questions about PII handling, VPC peering, and measurable latency for short biomedical prompts. Agreed pilot with sample dataset and two-week benchmarking window.
action_items: Maya Kim - Send tailored pilot pricing and sample SOW - 2026-07-20
Samir Patel - Provide a runnable example repo with field-mapper schema + tool plugin for HavenBio's enrichment API - 2026-07-22
Dr. Elena Ruiz - Share representative prompt corpus and schema mapping expectations (anonymized) - 2026-07-18
Tom Berger - Confirm network topology and whether VPC peering or Private deployment is required for pilot - 2026-07-21
next_steps: Schedule pilot kickoff: two-week latency/cost benchmark using 100k tokens workload
Share security pack (SOC2, audit logs, KMS integration notes) via SSO-restricted link
Set up a short tech sync to run initial end-to-end call with HavenBio enrichment API
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-15
Time: 16:00 UTC / 09:00 PT
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Kim (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Dr. Elena Ruiz (HavenBio), Tom Berger (HavenBio), Anika Shah (HavenBio CTO)
Link: deck shared (drive.redwood/example-field-mapper-demo) security pack (redwood.com/security/havenbio)

[00:00] Maya Kim: Hi everyone, thanks for making time. Quick intros — Im Maya, I run platform partnerships here at Redwood. With me is Samir, our solutions engineer who will do the demo.

[00:18] Anika Shah: Thanks Maya. Were excited — short background: HavenBio builds NLP pipelines over clinical notes and lab reports, so consistency and PII handling are musts.

[00:30] Samir Patel: Great. Today we'll show JSON mode plus a "field-mapper" pattern we've been working on — basically enforcing output schemas, wiring tool calls for enrichment, and runtime routing to model variants with fallbacks. Ill start with the API contract then jump into the Console and a live run.

[00:50] Dr. Elena Ruiz: Couple of things up front: our prompts are short, often <100 tokens. Latency is critical. Also some outputs must never include raw PHI. Weve got an internal enrichment API that annotates and redacts, ideally would like Redwood to call it as a tool.

[01:12] Maya Kim: Totally — thats a very common pattern. Weve done that with a few healthcare customers. We provide tool-calling primitives and you can define an external tool endpoint; we support VPC-hosted connectors for Private deployments or a secure peered tunnel for Dedicated.

[01:36] Tom Berger: On the security side we need KMS integration for key management and very granular audit logs mapped to user IDs. Is that in the security pack?

[01:46] Maya Kim: Yep, well send the security pack. It details KMS/HSM options, audit log retention tiers, and RBAC controls. We'll include examples of audit log formats so you can map them to your SIEM.

[02:05] Samir Patel: Jumping in — first slide: JSON mode. The idea is you supply a schema, and the model must produce strictly-typed JSON. We surface partial validation errors and deterministic fallbacks if the model strays.

[02:28] Dr. Elena Ruiz: When you say deterministic fallback, do you mean an immediate retry with a constrained prompt or do you have transform layers?

[02:36] Samir Patel: Both. You can define validation rules (required fields, regex, enums) and a fallback policy. Example policy: if schema fails, we first try a constrained re-prompt (prompt + few-shot examples); if still failing, route to a smaller locally quantized variant with a stricter sampling config, or call a deterministic post-processor to coerce types. You can chain these steps.

[03:05] Anika Shah: Hmm — do you have a notion of "field-mapping"? We want to remap vendor names and clinical codes into our internal ontology.

[03:14] Samir Patel: Yes — field-mapper is a runtime transform that maps output fields into your canonical IDs via a look-up tool. In the demo Ill wire a simple enrichment tool that takes predicted term and returns a canonical code and confidence.

[03:30] Maya Kim: Quick qualification — what's your pilot timeline and success criteria?

[03:36] Dr. Elena Ruiz: Two-week pilot would be ideal. Success metrics: 95% schema-conformant outputs, end-to-end p95 latency under 700ms for 100-token prompts, and zero raw PHI in model output — everything must hit enrichment tool before persistence.

[03:58] Maya Kim: Good, thats concrete. We can run throughput across dedicated reserved slots or a hosted pilot with routing to dedicated if you need SLAs.

[04:10] Samir Patel: Demo time. Im switching to the Console — youll see a policy editor. First Im uploading a JSON Schema for a "patient_summary" object: name is intentionally excluded, diagnosis_code enum, findings array with objects (term, confidence), and source_redacted boolean.

[04:36] [screen share noise] Samir Patel: Heres the field-mapper config: tool_tap -> enrichment_api (POST /enrich). For each findings[].term we execute the tool and populate findings[].canonical_code and findings[].vendor_confidence. The tool call is batched per request if there are multiple terms.

[04:58] Dr. Elena Ruiz: Is the tool call synchronous? Were concerned about added latency hitting our enrichment service.

[05:06] Samir Patel: Its synchronous by default to preserve strict ordering, but you can mark tool calls as async/non-blocking for eventual enrichment, or use a cached mapping to avoid network calls for high-frequency terms. We also have local prefix/KV caching to short-circuit common values.

[05:28] Tom Berger: Ok, caching is good. We run a lot of identical lab terms — would prefer the cache to live in your dedicated runtime rather than call our network for every token.

[05:38] Samir Patel: Thats supported on Dedicated; we can pre-populate a cache with your lookup table. For the pilot we can set a small TTL and seed it with your top 10k terms.

[05:50] [06:00] Samir Patel: Now Im going to run a live example via the API from the Console. The prompt: "Summarize the note and list findings" — short 48-token input. Response will be in JSON mode using the schema.
[06:12] [06:20] Speaker 1 (automated): call start

[06:21] Samir Patel: Hitting the endpoint now... (typing) Ok response streaming in. Ill drop the raw model output first — you can see the model attempted free text then produced a JSON blob. Validation failed: findings[0].canonical_code missing. Our policy triggered a tool call to enrichment_api and revalidated. Final payload -- shows canonical_code populated and source_redacted true.

[06:50] Dr. Elena Ruiz: Nice. Can you show the logs for that request? We want to see the token cost, latency per step, and the tool call trace.

[06:58] Samir Patel: Sure — Console -> request trace. You can see timings: model generation 420ms, tool call 160ms, validation 12ms, serialization 8ms, total 600ms. Token cost breakdown is visible: prompt 12 tokens, generation 54 tokens.

[07:22] Anika Shah: Those numbers are promising. For production we'd need p95 guarantees. If we use Dedicated Reserved, what are the latency SLOs?

[07:30] Maya Kim: With Dedicated and reserved GPU pools we offer latency targets based on model class and sequence length; for short prompts (<=100 tokens) you can expect sub-700ms p95 on our v2 small-optimized runtimes. We include a SLA in the contract.

[07:48] Dr. Elena Ruiz: About PHI: you said enrichment runs pre-persistence. But can we ensure that the model never returns raw PHI in any field accidentally?

[07:58] Samir Patel: Two ways: 1) schema enforcement + post-validation prevents illegal fields from being returned, and 2) we can insert an in-line redaction tool as the first step — a deterministic redactor that strips or tokenizes PHI before final output. Also you can enforce a policy that any potential PHI is routed to a customer-owned enrichment tool running in your VPC for canonicalization before storage.

[08:26] Tom Berger: For pilot wed prefer the enrichment tool to be inside our network. How would the Private deployment differ?

[08:34] Maya Kim: In Private you run a customer-controlled control plane and optionally the serving plane in your VPC; tool calls to your enrichment service stay inside your network. We can help deploy the runtime as an appliance or Kubernetes chart. Audit trail lives in your account and KMS keys never leave.

[08:52] Dr. Elena Ruiz: Any limitations on function/tool calling semantics? Like nested calls, batch size limits?

[09:00] Samir Patel: You can chain calls, but we recommend keeping per-request tool call budgets reasonable — we typically advise <10 calls per request for latency-sensitive workflows. Batching of tool calls is automatic when the pattern is identical; the runtime groups them to save round trips.

[09:20] [09:30] Samir Patel: Back to the Console — Im going to flip to the policy editor to show fallback policy graphically. For this config: primary model = rdx-1.1 (hosted performant), fallback = rdx-q4f (quantized local), ultimate = deterministic post-processor. For routing we add a cost threshold so if cost per 1k tokens exceeds X we route lower.

[09:58] Dr. Elena Ruiz: Can we force certain customers or routes to never use quantized variants for quality reasons?

[10:06] Samir Patel: Yes — per-route pinning. You can pin by customer/team/model combo. For example production-critical routes can be pinned to unquantized variants and flagged for manual review if fallbacks trigger.

[10:20] Tom Berger: On the topic of A/B, can we run canary to compare unquantized vs quantized on a sampled percentage?

[10:26] Samir Patel: Absolutely — we have rollouts and canaries. You can route 5% of traffic to a candidate model and track regression metrics against your eval sets. The console ties model outputs back to prompt ids so diffing is straightforward.

[10:40] Anika Shah: Show me the evals panel.

[10:44] Samir Patel: Here — evals list: we import your prompt set, run both models, and compute schema-pass rate, string similarity, and task-specific metrics. You can set regression alerts.

[10:58] Dr. Elena Ruiz: Great. A few practicalities: we use SAML SSO and have multiple teams needing different RBAC. How granular is RBAC for the Console?

[11:08] Maya Kim: Very granular. You can provision roles per-route, per-model, and restrict who can edit fallbacks or rollouts. We can hook into your IdP; the security pack shows examples.

[11:24] Tom Berger: Ok can we talk about costs: were price-sensitive. How do you show unit economics with tool calls and caching?

[11:32] Samir Patel: Console gives token-level cost breakdown (prompt vs generation) and per-request tool call cost. With caching you'll see fewer external calls and less cost. Our Optimize module suggests a quantization profile and batching parameters to hit a target cost per 1k tokens while meeting latency SLOs.

[11:52] [12:00] Anika Shah: For telemetry, can we pull traces into our Datadog?

[12:04] Maya Kim: Yes — traces can be exported; we also provide webhooks for request events and a log connector for Datadog or Splunk.

[12:14] Samir Patel: Im going to do one more live flow, this time intentionally fail schema to show fallback chain. (typing) Feed prompt that elicits ambiguous phrasing; model returns free text again, fails schema validation, auto re-prompt with clarifying example, still fails, then we route to quantized fallback with deterministic sampling. The console flags the request and shows a diff tab with side-by-side JSONs.

[12:46] Dr. Elena Ruiz: That's useful — in production we'd like those flagged requests to create automatic tickets in our issue tracker. Any built-in integrations?

[12:54] Samir Patel: Built-in integrations for Jira, PagerDuty, Slack; you can also forward events to a webhook to connect to other systems.

[13:10] Tom Berger: About the enrichment tool code — can you drop a simple plugin example? We need to match our auth scheme (mTLS + token).

[13:18] Samir Patel: Ill attach a repo after the call. The plugin supports mTLS, token, or VPC private endpoints. It includes a sample that returns canonical_code and vendor_confidence.

[13:32] Anika Shah: For pilot scope — will you run the benchmark in our region? Were on GCP us-central1.

[13:38] Maya Kim: Yes, we have hosted regions and can allocate Dedicated capacity in GCP us-central1 for the pilot. For Private we can run in your region as well.

[13:50] [14:00] Dr. Elena Ruiz: Anything else we should know about failure modes? e.g., if the enrichment tool is down mid-request, what happens?

[14:06] Samir Patel: Policies let you configure: fail-open, fail-closed, or queue for async enrichment. For PHI-sensitive routes youd likely choose fail-closed or route to a cached fallback. We also support automatic retries with exponential backoff and circuit breakers per-tool-endpoint.

[14:30] Tom Berger: Good. Wed prefer fail-closed for now.

[14:36] Samir Patel: Noted.

[14:40] [15:00] Maya Kim: Lets do a quick recap and next steps. Elena — youll share an anonymized prompt corpus and desired schema mapping by Friday?

[15:08] Dr. Elena Ruiz: Yes, I can get that by 2026-07-18.

[15:12] Maya Kim: Samir will send an example repo and a seeded cache approach; Ill send pricing and SOW.

[15:22] Samir Patel: Ill also include the sample plugin demonstrating mTLS and token-based auth.

[15:28] Anika Shah: Wed like to see an estimate for total cost of ownership for the pilot vs in-house self-run. Do you have benchmarking numbers comparing your hosted runtime to a typical self-hosted quantized runtime?

[15:40] Samir Patel: We have a benchmark sheet — Ill include a tailored comparison using your estimated traffic. Quick note: for short prompts the overhead of network is significant; Dedicated reduces that and we can optimize batching and caching to hit your cost targets.

[15:56] Tom Berger: One more nit: data retention. We need an option to not persist prompts or to aggressively truncate logs for compliance.

[16:04] Maya Kim: Yes — retention is configurable per-route; you can set ephemeral mode for certain channels where we only store minimal telemetry. Thats in the security pack.

[16:16] [16:30] Dr. Elena Ruiz: Sounds good. Ill coordinate with Tom on the network posture doc.

[16:20] Maya Kim: Any other blockers?

[16:22] Anika Shah: Nothing else from me. Interested to see the repo and sample data.

[16:28] Maya Kim: Great — thanks everyone. Well follow up with the materials and get a calendar invite for the pilot kickoff.

[16:36] [16:40] Speaker 1 (automated): call end

Notes on transcription: occasional mislabels and filler removed for readability; original audio had a minor drop around 00:06:50 when the live run spiked network.
